evidence_summary: A 1970 Burnstein-Applebee catalog identifies the product as the Bowman Electronics Fuzz Maker Sound Kit. Contemporary electronics coverage identifies Bowman Mod-U-Kits as kits that could use circuit boards or point-to-point construction. This establishes Bowman as the marketed kit maker, not Applied Audio as the builder.

Tone Machines notes the kit contained an enclosure, PCB, wires and components, and that Bowman was based in Roselle/Garwood. The source explicitly reports no concrete link to Applied Audio or Trans-Tek and presents component-supply/old-stock connections only as hypotheses. The physical builder therefore remains Bowman-associated but not independently established at the component-assembly level.

Contemporary advertising identifies Bowman Leisure Industries of Garwood, New Jersey as the maker/distributor of Mod-U-Kits, while Electronics Illustrated describes Bowman Electronics Mod-U-Kits as widely distributed and using multiple construction methods. This supports a direct Bowman kit-product business identity.

Bowman and Trans-Tek were geographically close in Garwood, and Trans-Tek was known for surplus/bulk components and project kits. Tone Machines proposes possible cooperation or old-stock component supply, but explicitly states that no concrete link has been found. Proximity is not treated as manufacturing evidence.

The photographed Bowman fuzz reportedly shares some early Applied-style knobs and lamp hardware, but the enclosure labeling differs and appears purpose-built for the Bowman kit. Tone Machines therefore raises the possibility of reused components rather than an Applied circuit or assembly. No promotion is justified.
